title: Nvidia’s Project G-Assist AI: No More Googling For Help With Games?
text:
Nvidia is working on a new AI assistant that might mean you never need Google for help with a game again.
Dubbed Project G-Assist, the AI assistant will appear as an overlay while you’re playing games, allowing gamers to ask questions about the title they’re playing. The AI will be “context aware”, meaning it can see your current progress in the game and recommend actions that are relevant to that stage in proceedings.
Nvidia demonstrated the technology with ARK: Survival Ascended, a game in which the player finds themselves trapped on a prehistoric island with dinosaurs and other beasts, and must find a way to survive.
The demo showed a player asking questions such as: “what’s the best early-game weapon and where do I find the crafting materials for it?”. The AI assistant instantly advised that the best early-game weapon was a spear.
The AI was also able to understand which resources the player had gathered, allowing it to make recommendations about which crafting recipes to unlock next, for example.
So, will this be the death knell for content creators who publish game guides and wikis that help players progress through games? “In the future, we envision these assistants will be implemented by game developers and also by the communities themselves,” said Jesse Clayton, director of product marketing for Windows AI at Nvidia, adding that the company would also seek to work with “wiki sites, press sites who have guides and walkthroughs and lots of knowledge about specific games.”
He also hinted that the AI wouldn't go rogue and show players how to cheat at games, for example, by adding that Nvidia would work in “collaboration with game developers to ensure that these assistants align with developer objectives for the game.”
Project G-Assist isn’t the first AI assistant to provide gaming advice. Alternatives such as ChatGPT are already capable of helping gamers with specific queries about a game or to provide starter guides for newcomers to a particular title.
The key difference with Nvidia’s offering is that the player won’t need to leave the game to seek help. Project G-Assist appears as an overlay inside the game, meaning the player doesn’t have to pause the action or switch windows to get AI advice.
Game Performance Boosts
Project G-Assist won’t only provide gameplay tips and tricks, it will also help PC players tweak the performance of their computer hardware.
‘The AI understands your system and can help tune and optimize it for you,” said Clayton. “It can provide insights into performance metrics like fps [frames per second] and PC latency, for example, and track these for you as you tweak your PC for more responsiveness.”
The AI can also scan the PC to ensure that the player is, for example, taking full advantage of their display’s capabilities. “It may suggest optimal graphics settings for your particular setup, or even overclocking, or find ways to consume less power while maintaining a target of 60fps,” Clayton added.
Project G-Assist is merely a tech demonstration at this stage, with Nvidia not yet prepared to reveal when the AI assistant will be made available to the public or how much it might cost.
Project G-Assist is just one of a series of announcements Nvidia is making at the Computex tech show in Taipei this week, including enhancements to its software that allows games developers to create AI-driven characters in games and a new initiative to standardize graphics cards for small form-factor PCs.

title: 5 Ways AI Is Revolutionizing Traditional Foraging Practices
text:
Have you ever wondered about the hidden treasures growing in your own backyard or local park? Foraging—the practice of gathering edible wild food, whether flora, funga or fauna—has connected us to nature and our culinary roots for centuries. Now, AI has entered the world of foraging, bringing both promising advancements and significant risks. As a forager and plant-based chef, I've witnessed AI reshaping this ancient practice firsthand.
The question is, how accurate are these tools? Given the inaccuracies, what are the deep concerns with misidentification? In 2023 alone, news erupted about AI-generated foraging books taking over the web—and they were downright dangerous, often incorrectly identifying various plants and mushrooms. There is still much work to be done to negate concerns such as misidentification and misleading handbooks created by AI, where the outcomes can be devastating. Here are five ways AI is revolutionizing traditional foraging practices and why you should pay attention.
AI-Powered Identification Tools
AI-powered apps like PictureThis, iNaturalist and Picture Mushroom provide instant identification of plants and mushrooms by analyzing user-uploaded photos against their databases using proprietary AI. Now, even your iPhone has a plant identification tool built into the camera app to help you identify plants in seconds, and if you aren’t an iPhone owner, you can utilize tools like Google Lens. This accessibility is invaluable for novice foragers, offering a seemingly quick and easy way to learn about the natural world which can make foraging more approachable and exciting.
Though these apps are helpful, they don’t come without concerns. The accuracy of these tools is not always reliable. A 2024 study by the University of Michigan found that the top-ranked app, PictureThis, had a 73% accuracy rate and was overall helpful 89% of the time, averaging across all plant categories. While the results are promising, the inaccuracy gap can lead to dangerous misidentifications, particularly with toxic plants and fungi such as pokeweed or the destroying angel mushroom.
Each phone app typically gives users several suggestions for species-level identification, which tends to have more discrepancies than genus-level identification. When I began my foraging journey, I used PlantSnap to help identify maple trees for homemade maple syrup. Though it did not always accurately identify the species by the bark alone, it accurately identified the genus, Acer, which helped narrow down the identifiers. Leaf identification proved more accurate, often leading to correct species results, such as sugar maple versus black maple, crucial for understanding sugar content for syrup production.
There can be serious risks involved with misidentification in the field–including hospitalizations and at times, death–which highlights the serious risks involved with relying solely on AI based applications. Always cross-reference multiple sources. Field guides and books by experienced foragers, such as Samuel Thayer or Alan Bergo, remain the most reliable sources of accurate information. Consult experienced foragers or join expert-led workshops for safety. In Connecticut, the Foraging Club offers field trips to learn about local ecosystems and edible plants, an incredibly helpful and safe way to learn.
So, should these apps be used at all? In my opinion, yes, but as an aid to guide users rather than a definitive source. To be a well-rounded forager, you need basic plant identification skills and must understand the importance of double-checking plant species suggestions provided by an app. Dr. Julie Peacock, Associate Professor of Ecology at the University of Galway, summarizes the why perfectly: “A calculator is an excellent tool in math, but without knowledge of at least basic arithmetic, someone using it could not know if the calculator was giving a strange answer. Similarly, basic plant identification skills and a willingness to check suggestions that apps make will help the individual most effectively use these apps.”
Digital Archives of Traditional Knowledge and Addressing Climate Change with AI
AI can help create comprehensive digital archives of traditional foraging knowledge, preserving cultural practices for future generations. Indigenous knowledge, often transmitted orally or through traditional practices, is vulnerable to eradication. Initiatives like the Indigenous Digital Archive use AI to document and preserve this knowledge, ensuring these invaluable resources are not lost to time. Imagine having access to centuries of foraging wisdom at your fingertips, allowing you to connect with nature in a deeper, more informed way.
From a climate perspective, Indigenous people are known as the “stewards of the land” worldwide. Centering their perspectives when contemplating AI structures is crucial when attempting to utilize these tools as a means of fighting the climate crisis. Take for example the Ojibwe people native to Minnesota—they teach a deep message about sustainable and selective harvesting, encouraging people to take only what they need while leaving enough for the plants to regenerate and for animals to use.
These philosophies are necessary for AI models to take into account when attempting to provide climate solutions that are balanced from both an Indigenous epistemology and scientific standpoint. Between 2015 and 2019, 100 million hectares of healthy land were degraded each year. Moreover, nearly 1 million animal and plant species are currently at risk of extinction due to human activities. This underscores the biodiversity crises we face today, many of which directly affect our food systems from both a foraging and cultivation standpoint. Although Indigenous people comprise less than 5% of the world population, they protect 80% of earth's biodiversity.
According to the most recent UN Report on Biodiversity, nearly half the world's migratory species are in decline, with 97% of migratory fish species on the brink of extinction. Projects like PolArtics’ integration of Indigenous knowledge with AI in Nunavut demonstrate how AI can enhance understanding of local ecosystems and support sustainable practices in foraging and mariculture (marine farming). The pilot project, which started in 2021, uses satellite data, scientific research and AI to pioneer responses to climate change problems. It helps Indigenous communities in the Arctic locate previously undiscovered fishing locations and predict environmental changes that affect habitat growth and harvests.
Fishing holds immense significance in Indigenous cultures, encompassing economic, nutritional, cultural and spiritual dimensions. For many, it’s a primary food source, providing essential nutrients and proteins, especially in harsher climates. These practices are deeply intertwined with the cultural identity and traditions of Indigenous peoples, often passed down through generations. Tribes in the Pacific Northwest and Canada celebrate the return of salmon with ceremonies that honor both the fish—for providing them with sustenance—and the ecosystem. The Maori of New Zealand have traditional practices and laws governing fishing to ensure populations remain healthy and sustainable.
While digital archives are useful, they may lack the depth and nuance of hands-on experience. The richness of oral traditions and personal stories can be difficult to capture fully in a digital format. Moreover, Indigenous cultures often center their understanding and knowledge of the world through the lens of nature being one with man. Jason Edward Lewis, a Hawaiian and Samoan professor at Concordia University, notes that the Western approach to AI exploration creates blindness to vital aspects of human existence, such as trust, care and community, which he believes are fundamental to how intelligence operates. There is an overarching worry about the widening gap between diverse forms of human and non-human intelligence and how AI is being trained to only see life from a rational and calculated standpoint.
Indigenous theories of knowledge provide frameworks for advancing technology in ways that support and uplift culture, improve everyday life and promote abundance. Carolina Running Wolf, a Ph.D. student at the University of British Columbia, states, “AI is built by engineers that do not represent a cross-cut of society...” and continues, “It’s not just about bits and bytes, it’s the sacred stories and voices of our ancestors.”
The emotional depth of traditional storytelling and cultural preservation is often missing from digital archives. AI models may oversimplify the complexity of ecosystems, leading to recommendations that may not fully consider the intricate relationships between species, habitats and human activities. As technology evolves in its role in preserving cultural knowledge, placing Indigenous cultures at the decision-making table can push AI to be more inclusive overall.
Educational Resources and Accessibility
AI-driven platforms provide educational resources that make foraging more accessible. These tools can teach users about different plants and their uses, promoting a broader understanding of foraging practices. For instance, AI platforms have been integrated into educational programs, helping students learn about botany and ecology in an interactive way. Imagine turning a simple walk in the park into an educational treasure hunt, discovering edible plants you never knew existed.
In 2024, a study conducted by the National Library of Medicine involved fifth-grade students using a mobile application called PlantNet to learn new herbs and trees, encouraging out-of-classroom learning. Initially, students took a plant species questionnaire. After using the app in the field, they took the questionnaire again. The results were intriguing.
Students who participated in activities with PlantNet could write down more herb and tree species at the end of the activities. Moreover, a positive and high-level relationship was found between the students’ biodiversity-related behaviors and the total number of plant species they knew. This indicates that while AI-enabled apps are not always effective, they can increase knowledge and encourage outdoor exploration when done right.
However, relying solely on AI for education can result in a superficial understanding. True expertise requires a combination of digital tools and traditional learning methods, such as field guides, books by experienced foragers, and in-person workshops. Experiential learning is crucial for developing a deep understanding of plant identification and foraging techniques. Competent field biologists are visual experts, often able to identify plants at a glance.
Promoting Sustainable Foraging Practices
AI can promote sustainable foraging by offering guidelines and tips on responsible harvesting. It can enhance knowledge preservation, optimize resource management and support conservation efforts. Apps like PlantSnap provide information on sustainable foraging practices and the ecological impact of harvesting certain plants, such as the beloved ramp, which takes seven years to grow from seed and whose population is in question in certain parts of the U.S.
The app provides tips such as only harvesting one leaf per plant or avoiding digging up the ramp bulbs in scarce locations, helping protect natural ecosystems and ensuring that foraging practices do not deplete local plant populations. By following these guidelines, you can enjoy foraging while contributing to the preservation of our natural resources. Earlier, I mentioned PolArctic being used to help Indigenous people assess fishing conditions, but it is also noteworthy that this AI model conducts deep documentation on plant species and their uses, sustainable harvesting techniques and seasonal patterns.
While AI can provide guidelines, it cannot enforce them. Sustainable foraging requires a deep understanding of local ecosystems, which AI may not fully capture. Ethical foraging also involves respect for Indigenous practices and knowledge.
Foraging Books Written by AI Are Taking Over
AI can inspire new ways of thinking about foraging by suggesting novel uses for foraged ingredients and innovative recipes. This fusion of technology and tradition can lead to exciting culinary creations that honor the past while embracing the future. AI-generated recipes using foraged ingredients have inspired chefs to experiment with new dishes that blend traditional and modern techniques and expand their imagination. Envision transforming wild plants into gourmet meals, bringing a touch of nature to your dining table.
However, there is a significant risk that AI-generated foraging books and recipes may provide inaccurate or dangerous information. The controversy surrounding AI-generated content highlights the need for careful oversight and validation by human experts. In 2023, a wave of AI-generated foraging books on Amazon caused significant controversy and stirred the foraging community.
Digital books such as The Forager’s Harvest Bible, The Edible Wild Plants Bible, and others were published and utilized by many, some even garnering hundreds of reviews. To a new or even seasoned forager looking for a new book to read, they may have looked appealing at first glance, with AI-generated author photos to match. Upon closer inspection, however, there was no trace of the authors. Moreover, when reading through some pages of these books, many seemed to mimic the style or inspiration of renowned foragers such as Samuel Thayer, undermining years of work and dedication to the trade while providing misinformation.
These AI-generated books clearly showcased a lack of nuanced knowledge, suggesting that readers should taste mushrooms and plants as a means of identification—something that can lead to hospitalization or even death if someone eats say, a death cap mushroom or poison hemlock. Professor Myron Smith, a fungi specialist at Carleton University in Canada, called the books “totally irresponsible” and noted that some differences between edible and non-edible species are too subtle, requiring an experienced eye to tell the difference.
While AI can enhance accessibility, education and sustainability, it also comes with its fair share of concerns. Embrace AI as a tool, but always respect the wisdom and experience central to the human forager, cultural knowledge and field guides above all else.

title: 7 Cultural Trends For 2024 And Beyond
text:
We live in a state of transition. The current system isn’t working but the future is uncertain. In the words of Antonio Gramsci: “The crisis consists precisely in the fact that the old is dying and the new cannot be born.”
Despite the introduction of the automobile by Karl Benz in 1886, more than 130,000 horses worked in Manhattan in 1900. The invention of the telephone by Alexander Graham Bell in 1876 didn’t stop people from using the telegraph until the mid-20th century. In 2024, 54% of Americans wrote a check. Meanwhile, two thirds of Gen-Z use peer-to-peer mobile payment apps like Venmo, Cash App and PayPal.
Contrary to popular belief, the new doesn’t replace the old. We are in limbo: a messy and protracted neverland where new ideas and old systems wrestle for oxygen. The 2025-2030 period will prove formative to the future of business and society. Here are seven cultural trends that will shape the next decade.
New adulthood
The traditional markers of adulthood are no longer achievable or aspirational. Young people aged 16 to 24 are more likely to work in unstable jobs within the gig economy. Homeownership is down in most developed countries. Nearly 50% of young adults (18 to 29) in the U.S. and 30% of young adults in the U.K. (25 to 29) live with their parents. Marriage is on the decline and only 55% of Gen-Z and Millennials plan to have children. Birth rates are falling in Japan, South Korea, the European Union, China and the U.K.
Using the traditional metrics, young people are growing up at a slower pace than previous generations. But young people’s economic reality is incommensurable with the post-WWII generation. There is a fluidity and uncertainty to modern life which can’t be accurately captured in these linear life stages. Millennials and Gen-Z are the first generation worse off than their parents. Wage stagnation, job insecurity and a shortage in housing have created a generational wealth gap. The work hard, you’ll succeed promise is broken.
The notion of life stages is being challenged and reshaped. There is no longer a neatly defined beginning, middle and end. Companies can’t afford to plan future activities using out-of-date demographic data. Using data such as age, marital status and homeownership to make decisions is at best useless, and at worse misleading. Brands need to co-create with communities and conduct qualitative research to understand the shared values, interests and motivations of their ideal audience.
Virtual empires
The invention of steam-powered machinery in the 18th century enabled the manufacturing economy. We shifted away from small production to mass production. Private enterprises made fortunes selling goods and services for a higher price than it cost them to produce. In 1997, the world’s most valuable companies were General Electric, Coca-Cola and Royal Dutch Shell. General Electric sold home appliances, Royal Dutch Shell sold oil and gas and The Coca-Cola Company sold carbonated soft drinks. On the surface, these companies don’t have much in common. But all three sold a physical product using raw materials, factories and workers. The process was labor-intensive and required enormous capital expenditure to achieve economies of scale.
The financial crisis of 2008 transformed the shape of our economy. In 2024, the most valuable companies are Microsoft, Apple, Nvidia, Google and Amazon. Unlike the traditional manufacturing economy of the 1990s, we are operating under the reign of virtual empires. Using technology, machine learning algorithms and direct marketing: virtual empires can bypass competition and extract maximum rent from consumers. Only 4% of Microsoft’s revenue comes from devices, and most (34%) comes from server products and cloud services. Apple Services is the fastest-growing product and now represents 24% of revenue. Google services generated 90% of Alphabet’s revenue with the remaining 9% being Google Cloud. Amazon private label products represent 1% of total revenue. Whilst Amazon Web Services (AWS) is the most profitable segment of the business.
The traditional advertising model of generating demand is less influential. Algorithms have broken the marketing funnel. Brands should explore subscription offerings that expand beyond the production of physical products and deliver ongoing value.
Citizen rebellion
During the pandemic, companies were facing unprecedented community pressure to ramp up racial justice and social equity. Corporations promised $200 billion for racial justice initiatives following the murder of George Floyd in 2020. The sudden change in discourse and mindset went beyond tackling racism. It suggested that companies can play a constructive role in society.
Companies advocated for stakeholder capitalism: that corporations should serve the needs of all stakeholders including employees, customers and communities, not just shareholders. At the same time, we witnessed increased interest in ESG from institutional investors. But now we are seeing a backlash against so-called woke corporate capitalism. As seen with Bud Light backlash and Target removing its annual pride collection. ESG and DEI are now in decline both in terms of investment and workforce allocation. Companies are more wary of making a stand. At the same time, the call for brands to make a stand is as strong as ever. Especially for Gen-Z who are hyper-informed, globally connected and socially conscious. Both McDonald’s and Starbucks have recently taken a significant hit on share prices and missed key sales targets for their perceived support of the war in Gaza.
Brands are stuck in the middle, having to navigate an increasingly charged and polarized political atmosphere. Not taking a stand will alienate both parties and taking a stand might activate the wrath of the opposing group. This is especially problematic for mass-market consumer brands that need to appeal to everyone. Society is fragmented across socio-economic and ideological divides. All things being equal, challenger brands with a defined mission will outperform generic brands without a cause. Companies should work to unite people rather than exacerbate differences.
AI companions
AI is the hottest thing since the internet. It has the same buzz as the metaverse but with more practical applications. According to the IMF, almost 40% of global employment is exposed to AI. Companies will replace human labour with AI once the technology is more productive and less expensive. But this isn’t the biggest challenge. AI is exponential. It can produce and reproduce content based on human input. For the last 10,000 years, humans have been the main decision-makers dominating the destiny of our planet. Could the next 100 years look drastically different?
This is not a dystopian sci-fi novel. Humans are opting to interact with AI software over other human beings. Pi the AI assistant has more than 6 million monthly active users. Young women in China are turning to AI boyfriends because they are more kind, empathetic and understand them better than real men. Young people are embracing AI therapists since its cheap, quick, anonymous and available 24/7. We may never need human cooperation in the same way. AI companions can be calibrated to meet our needs and desires without the need to communicate, compromise or engage with messy humans.
Social cooperation has been the foundation of human civilization for millennia. Could AI companionship transform how society is organized? We might begin to see two forms of society. One society where humans and AI are companions and another which remains human-led. One of the blessings and curses of humanity is that we create new technologies before we understand their repercussions.
Inter-nationalism
Nationalism is filling a void left by global uncertainty and turmoil. Last year I wrote about global fragmentation: “For the first time since the collapse of the Soviet Union, we are witnessing the emergence of a new bipolar system. A fragmented world governed by opposing factions and competing spheres of influence. Unrestrained globalization seems like an outlier as we head back into a more disjointed world.”
The prevailing narrative was a global economy powered by free markets and progressive politics. Many people have stopped believing in the story of globalization. This is particularly true of communities who feel locked out of global markets. As seen with Brexit, growing nationalization in India and a new wave of nationalism in Europe. There is now a concerted move to move back to the good old days. Global collaboration has drastically improved human development. More people die from obesity today than from malnutrition. More people die from suicide than war. And more people die from old age than from disease. We have made tremendous progress, but the benefits haven’t been distributed equally.
We can’t tackle global problems with unilateral action. Let’s take the climate breakdown as an example. There are estimated to be 1.2 billion climate refugees by 2050. Even if nations choose not to reduce or change their policies, they will still see the impact of the climate crisis. The battle between global cooperation and national identity was visible during the global pandemic when nation-states prioritized vaccines for their own country and local region above global needs. The world is interconnected and interdependent. We need international principles and local solutions.
Lost imagination
Perhaps the greatest marker of the late 2010s and early 2020s is our reliance on historical memory. During the Renaissance, people were searching for new answers. The period was characterized by boundless curiosity and discovery. Artists, scientists and scholars were actively looking for new solutions and wealthy benefactors were willing to sponsor their endeavours. Today, we seem to be more comfortable replaying or remixing old songs than creating new sounds.
We have more movie sequels than ever before in history. In the 1990s, just 11.7% of the domestic box office went to sequels, whereas in the ten years between 2014 and 2023, it was an average of 41.7%. Not only does this demonstrate a lack of creativity but a prevailing culture of playing it safe and being rewarded for the familiar rather than exploring the unknown. From an audience perspective, the familiarity of existing ideas, narratives and norms makes people feel less comfortable amidst an uncertain world. A similar trend could be seen with the rise of Y2K fashion and Gen-Z channelling the 1990s core.
The yearning for nostalgia conceals a lack of imagination. If companies, producers and creators continue to feed this nostalgia we end up in an unimaginativeness feedback loop. We need leaders who have the vision to create new stories rather than mimic the old. With everything that’s happened in the last five years—the first global pandemic in a century, looming planetary destruction and multiple wars—it feels like we have given up on the future. Brands that can show imagination and originality will become new-age leaders.
Next-gen innovation
Across the globe, multinational corporations are cutting costs and getting back to profitability. Leaders are working hard to align budgets with slower revenue growth. Nonetheless, leaders shouldn’t sacrifice long-term ambitions for short-term gains. The greatest danger is not being prepared for the future. There is little point in short-term cost reduction without a clearly defined strategy. Having a shared vision for the future makes all cost-cutting and investment activities strategic, not tactical. You can begin to build brand equity and connect with future consumers. Without a future strategy, cutting costs to post better-than-expected quarterly returns could be a downward spiral to extinction.
Brands need to constantly update, innovate and reinvent themselves. Even the world’s most valuable and famous brand Nike has struggled due to lack of product innovation. The company focused too much on the past—and the success of its most iconic cultural lines like Air Force 1 and Air Jordan 1—that it stopped investing in the future. As consumer markets become more saturated, competitive and sluggish. Embracing product innovation and new audiences can be the engine of marketing growth. Companies need to seek new opportunities and unchartered territories. Today’s best practice is tomorrow’s dead end.

title: 8 Helpful High-Income Skills That Are Safe From AI In 2024
text:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is generating buzz both for what it can do and who it might replace, but certain high-income jobs remain firmly in the domain of human expertise. These roles demand a unique blend of social and emotional intelligence, creativity, and critical thinking.
Artificial Intelligence has certainly unburdened a lot of the tasks and helped tremendously in simplifying the workload. For example, salespeople are using AI to analyze sales calls faster, bloggers and content creators are already using AI to streamline the writing process, and customer support reps are bringing customers faster solutions. Despite being so good with almost all job roles, there are still some jobs that AI can’t replace. These include jobs that require creativity, empathy, critical thinking, and human interaction.
8 Skills That Remain Safe From AI Takeover In 2024
So which jobs should you consider if you want to prepare yourself financially for the AI revolution? Here are a few options.
Software Development: Work With AI
The field of software development, often regarded as a hotbed of AI advancement, is a profession where humans and machines need to work together. While AI can draft code, creative problem-solving and innovative thinking are where you need humans. AI can code to a certain degree like writing short command line programs and raw codes but creating hardcore coding is out of its range.
Also, you know that – Humans build AI; it’s not the other way around. Now that we are in the era of AI advancement, now is the time when skilled developers are needed the most.
Designing: Essence Of Human Touch
AI may do everything. But it cannot be as creative as humans. Humans possess the prerequisites of good design; perspective, vision, creativity, and feelings which a machine can never learn.
Yes, AI can generate visuals based on data, but it lacks the capacity for artistic expression, evoke emotions and the ability to give unique branding to a product.
Human Resources: A Human Response
Navigating workplace dynamics, understanding individual needs, and fostering a positive work environment are uniquely human skills
HR professionals excel in understanding people, resolving conflicts, and maintaining a positive work environment. While AI can assist with other administrative tasks, it cannot replace the interpersonal skills essential for HR.
Mental Health and Counseling: Providing Conversational Support
Therapists provide emotional support, coping strategies, and guidance to individuals dealing with mental issues. This can only be understood by another human with feelings.
They provide mental health support and require empathy active listening, and emotional intelligence – skills that AI currently struggles with.
Legal Professionals: The Nuances of Judgment And Advocacy
Legal experts, such as lawyers, advocates, and paralegals, engage in complex human judgment, intricate arguments, and ethical considerations. While AI can assist with legal research and fast-track law-reacted research, it cannot replicate the courtroom actions of judgment.
Legal expertise involves understanding context, cultural norms, and the art of persuasion – areas where human judgment excels.
Education: Shaping Minds with Human Learnings
Educators inspire, educate, and shape future generations. It has been this way for generations. Moreover, education isn’t only about what’s written in books. It is also empathy, compassion, respect, attitude and more.
While AI can facilitate personalized learning, it falls short of establishing the human connection that educators cultivate with their students.
A teacher not only builds the career of a child but also the character. However, even if it is all about bookish knowledge, every student needs different methodologies, which can only be met by a human.
Marketing: Strategic Insights And Emotional Intelligence
This is where storytelling and brand management become critical and hence, marketers occupy a distinct role. This is, again, one of the most important jobs that AI can’t replace.
AI may streamline data analysis and automate certain tasks like giving stats and results, yet it falters in understanding human emotions and constructing powerful brand narratives.
If you’re a marketer, you know how the decisions are based on human responses more than data. Also, marketers use their strategic thinking and brand ideas to build campaigns for the audiences, which is something can’t do.
Healthcare Professions: Mix of Compassion And Expertise
AI serves as a valuable auxiliary tool in healthcare, aiding in diagnoses and treatment recommendations. It has already fastened multiple healthcare operations like analyzing patient base, predicting future scenarios, etc.
The delicate nature of surgery and other medical procedures, combined with the need for human judgment and bedside manner, make these jobs irreplaceable by AI for now. It cannot replace the compassion and expertise of healthcare professionals, including doctors, nurses, therapists, and support staff.
As AI continues to thrive, these high-income jobs will remain secure due to their reliance on uniquely human skills. While technology enhances efficiency, it cannot replace the essence of what makes us human. In case you feel threatened by AI, you have two choices:
- Upskill and build your brand
- Change your career
I’d recommend the first.
